message.reasoning_content:
I'm looking at multi.py around line 1388, where an `IndexError` is caught, which hints the authors knew about this edge case. The only commit in the repo means git history won't help. For A, the suspicion is `tuples_to_object_array`, which sets its width from the first tuple's length, so longer tuples get truncated and shorter ones later raise `IndexError`. The list-path counterpart, `to_object_array_tuples`, uses the maximum width and pads instead, so I'm checking whether that difference is where the bad behavior starts.

Tracing the list path further, I see `pd.Index` with mixed-length tuples pads the shorter one with None, which becomes NaN, so that gives a 3-level MultiIndex. The team's plain-list `reindex` case goes through the same `tuples_to_object_array` truncation. With all-3-length keys, the target becomes a 3-level MultiIndex against a 2-level self, and `get_indexer` only recodes the first two levels, so matching ends up happening on those two levels alone.

The `_recode_for_new_levels` method only accepts a target with at least as many levels as self, so the extra level in the 3-level target gets silently dropped. A shorter first tuple would give a 1-level target and trip an assertion instead. I'm checking whether the bounds-checked indexing in `tuples_to_object_array` explains the `IndexError` case, since it's the one path that still lacks a clear explanation.

I'm weighing whether the faulty decision sits in the helper that builds tuple arrays, which is reached from `from_tuples` and from the plain-list reindex path, or in the level-recoding step that never checks the target's level count. The `[("a","b"),("b",)]` and `[1,1]` cases point to the first, while the `[0,1]` match on 3-tuples and the AssertionError for `[("b",),("a","b")]` point to the second. I still need to list every caller of the helper before deciding which one owns the decision.

I'm checking whether `from_tuples` is where the width gets fixed, since that's the only caller of `tuples_to_object_array`. Its ndarray/Index branch takes the width from the first element, and I'm listing which callers pass it those inputs: reindex, `map`, `append`, and a few others.

Checking the Cython helper `tuples_to_object_array` that builds the tuple grid, which sizes its width from the first tuple and reads each tuple by index up to that width.

Checking whether the upstream code has the same mismatched-length behavior, since the list and ndarray branches of `from_tuples` seem to handle widths differently and I want to know if this is a known issue.

I'm checking the installed package against the checkout, since the two seem to differ in logic, and I want to confirm which source I'm actually analyzing. The checkout is the one to trust here, so I'll work from its code to pin down which routine makes the faulty decision.

I'm weighing a narrower fix in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`: only convert to a MultiIndex when every tuple matches `self.nlevels`, otherwise keep the object Index so whole tuples compare as-is, which would make the mismatched keys return -1. That handles `get_indexer`, `reindex` and `loc`, but not the `from_tuples` duplicates or `Index.map`, which would need `tuples_to_object_array` to pad to the maximum width instead.

Checking whether the indexing path ever confirms that the target's level count matches self's; it seems the answer is no, and I'm looking at where `get_indexer` routes a MultiIndex target.

I'm checking whether the level-count check is missing from the indexing path, since `_recode_for_new_levels` only asserts that the target has no more levels than self and quietly ignores any extra ones. I'm also weighing the `loc` and `isin` cases, which fail differently from `get_indexer` and may point to where the wrong decision actually lives.

I'm noting that the isin check and the `_validate_key_length` path both reject wrong-length keys explicitly, so those cases are fine. Next I want to see whether `MultiIndex.get_loc` makes the same length check, since that would show where the unchecked indexing path diverges.

I'm settling on the root cause: `tuples_to_object_array` takes its width from the first tuple alone, so the width is set by `tuples[0]` and not by the rest of the keys. The list-path helper avoids this by using the maximum width, which makes me suspect the decision is really about which width gets chosen.

Next I'm checking the case where the first key is shorter than the rest, since `tuples_to_object_array` would size everything from that short first tuple and truncate the others.

I'm splitting this into two mechanisms: the width taken from the first tuple in `tuples_to_object_array`, which causes the truncation and the IndexError, and the MultiIndex lookup that never requires both sides to have the same number of levels, which silently ignores the extra target levels.

I'm settling on the idea that the indexing path has a single underlying flaw: a tuple target with three levels is matched against a two-level index without any length check, and the reported variants all come from tuple keys. I'm checking whether a fix in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` that only converts when every tuple has `nlevels` entries would cover the direct MultiIndex case too.

I'm checking what happens if `tuples_to_object_array` sizes its width from the longest tuple instead of the first, to see whether that alone would fix the `get_indexer` cases.

Even if the width in `tuples_to_object_array` were fixed to raise on ragged input, a uniform-width 3-level key list would still hit the unchecked MultiIndex lookup and return wrong matches. So a single change to that helper can't cover both mechanisms.

I'm settling on `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` as the decision point: it converts keys to a MultiIndex without checking that each tuple has `self.nlevels` entries, which would explain the get_indexer and reindex variants. The `from_tuples` duplicates and `Index.map` cases still need a separate explanation through `tuples_to_object_array`.

I'm now weighing whether the width-from-first-tuple choice in `tuples_to_object_array` is the real decision, and whether the 3-level case, which still returns [0, 1], needs its own explanation through the MultiIndex lookup.

I'm weighing whether to frame this as one root cause or two: the tuple-to-MultiIndex conversion never checks that each key has the indexed level count, and downstream recoding quietly ignores extra levels. I'll settle on which to present as the decision point.

Now I'm checking the remaining candidates for the repeated pattern, starting with the pivot code path, and I'm looking for other places that repeat the same inline expression.

I'm now checking whether the same expression, `self.where(mask)` and `other.where(mask)`, is repeated inline in other places, and I'm comparing those against what upstream pandas does in `_inplace_method`.

Those variants all trace back to tuple keys being converted into a MultiIndex without checking that each one has the indexed level count. I'm now weighing whether the repair belongs in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, or whether the width-from-first-tuple choice in `tuples_to_object_array` is the real decision. Upstream pandas appears to have the same bugs, so they look like genuine issues rather than something injected here.

I'm settling on the first-tuple width in `tuples_to_object_array` as the source for the from_tuples path, while the 3-level `get_indexer` case looks like it needs a length check in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` instead.

I'm tracing the indexing side: `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` hands the keys to `from_tuples`, which sizes everything from the first tuple, and the downstream recoding only checks that the target has at least as many levels as self. Next I'm wondering whether the inline `MultiIndex.from_...` conversion is repeated at other call sites as well.

I'm checking where else the inline `MultiIndex.from_tuples` conversion appears: `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, `_wrap_reindex_result`, and `_convert_can_do_setop`. `isin` already guards the length explicitly, which is why it behaves correctly. The `_wrap_reindex_result` path explains the duplicated `("a","b")` labels in the reindex output.

I'm settling on the root cause for this one: the number of levels is inferred from the first key and never checked against the index's own level count. Whether that decision lives in `tuples_to_object_array` or in the downstream recoding that silently drops extra levels is what I still need to pin down.

I'm weighing whether one fix in `tuples_to_object_array` could cover the from_tuples and Index.map symptoms by padding to the longest tuple, the way the list path already does. That still leaves the 3-level get_indexer case, which would need its own length check.

I'm testing whether a fix in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` that checks each key against `nlevels` would cover all the indexing variants at once, though the `from_tuples` and `Index.map` cases would still be left out.

I'm weighing whether the uniform three-level target still goes wrong through the level-recoding step, which only compares the first two levels, separately from the first-tuple width problem in the from_tuples path.

I'm settling on the tuple-key path as the single root cause: it never checks key length against the index's level count. The only place deciding how many levels the keys have is the first-tuple width in `tuples_to_object_array`, and downstream only a one-sided assertion guards it. So the repair belongs at the decision point in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, with a companion fix in the array helper for the `from_tuples` and `map` symptoms.

I'm settling on two separate flaws: the width is taken from the first tuple in `tuples_to_object_array`, and the downstream `_recode_for_new_levels` only asserts that the target has at least as many levels as self, so a three-level target gets read against just the first two levels.

Working out the repair now: a width-only fix in `tuples_to_object_array` can't cover the `get_indexer` case, since a three-level target still reads against just the first two levels. So I'm checking whether padding to the longest tuple, plus a level-count check downstream, handles both.

I'm now weighing a padding fix against the object fallback: padding would turn the 2-tuple into one with a NaN level and break the match, so the cleaner repair is to leave ragged keys out of the MultiIndex conversion in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`.

I'm concluding that the flaw is in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, which turns a tuple-keyed object Index into a MultiIndex without checking each key's length against `nlevels`. Ragged tuples don't make `from_tuples` raise, so the object fallback never gets a chance to run.

I'm now listing every caller of `MultiIndex.from_tuples`, since the only real consumer of the first-tuple width is that helper and `lib.tuples_to_object_array`. I want to know which of them can receive a plain ndarray or Index, because those are the inputs that take the width-from-first-tuple path.

I'm settling on four separate root causes, one per step, with the tuple-key path as the first: the key length is never checked against the MultiIndex's level count, so the shape gets decided entirely by the first key.

I'm planning to check line 2759 and how the get_indexer_non_unique path reaches get_indexer, since loc goes through _get_indexer_strict. I also want to run the proposed fix on a scratch copy outside the repo, and look at the isin and get_loc paths too.
